messages.author: bc3244d9806438a2
messages.subject: Phylogenetic methods for shape variables
parts:
What are currently viewed as the best practices for using shape variables to construct phylogenetic hypotheses? I’ve read a number of different methods in the literature and understand the limitations/issues with the applications, but admittedly lack the background to assess best (least worst?) options. The common options I’ve encountered include:

Neighbor joining on Procrustes distances
Maximum likelihood of continuous characters (PC scores, LDA scores, regular or transformed)
Weighted parsimony of scaled measurements

I’m specifically asking for extinct taxa where no molecular hypotheses exist, and taxa where continuous characters are more applicable than codeable ones. TIA.

Russ

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Phylogenetic methods for shape variables
parts:
Russ,

Under NO circumstances should one transform the shape variables before a statistical analysis, especially to obtain something like LDA scores.  LDA scores are statistical transformation that distort Procrustes distances among observations, meaning they do not convey shape difference.  (The distances among observations are statistic distances, which might be associated with group association.) To transform variables this way and then use them as data in another analysis is statistical chicanery that is sure to lead to spurious outcomes.

Maximum likelihood on PC scores is fine, but be aware that with shape data, the tendency to have ill-conditioned covariance matrices is great, so methods based on estimating likelihood are likely to lead to interpretive errors.  we discussed this recently: Adams and Collyer.  2018. Multivariate phylogenetic comparative methods: evaluations, comparisons, and recommendations. Systematic biology, 67(1), 14-31.

I do not see any problems with using squared-change parsimony to estimate ancestral character states or any clustering algorithm using Procrustes distances, unless, again  the method requires transforming variables in a strange way.  If you are wondering whether it is okay to build a tree based on Procrustes distances and compare it to a phylogenetic tree based on molecular data, that seems innocuous.  If you are wondering whether shape data can be used to infer models of evolution, that is a much more complicated question to answer, and one I will leave open for discussion.  (I think the answer is “yes” in theory but currently we have limited capacity to do it well.)

Hope that helps!
Mike

messages.author: 2fc03d53bc863e8d
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Phylogenetic methods for shape variables
parts: This is not a question about geomorph or even about geometric morphometrics except to the extent that the theory of shape is relevant for judging a method.  From that perspective, any method that requires you to pick a particular rotation of the data (such as principal components), and whose results depend on that choice, falls into the category of "most worst". But rotation-invariant methods might suffer from other problems, such as assuming a wildly unrealistic model for the evolution of shape.

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Phylogenetic methods for shape variables
parts:
Russ,

I interpreted Miriam’s comment to mean that problems that depend on the rotation of data are not unique to GM data, as via output from geomorph.  Some of the issues we point out in the reference I gave you is that alternative conclusions can be had from different data rotations (transformations).  For example, perform an analysis to determine the appropriate evolutionary model on Procrustes residuals.  Then do a PCA and perform the same analysis on PC scores.  There should be no difference in model likelihoods, thus no change in conclusion.  Some methods though will give different results/conclusions, as they are not rotation-invariant (and a rotation is one form of transformation).  Miriam added that even if a method is rotation-invariant, there could still be other inferential problems, if an unrealistic model of evolution is assumed.

I believe the point is that these issues are not unique to GM data, not that your question was inappropriate for this forum.  Your question started with “shape variables” but I think she was pointing out that if you asked the same questions with “sad clown variables”, the same concerns would be omnipresent.  At least that was my take.

Mike
